Testing - Pytest

Features of Pytest

4.  Gives useful failure information without the use of debuggers
5. Can be used to run doc tests and unit tests

Why Do We Need Python Environments?


  •  Different projects may require different Python or package
    versions

  •  Virtual environments isolate project dependencies from one
   another

  •  Benefits: avoids conflicts, improves reproducibility, protects
   system Python and simplifies deployment

  • Without isolation, upgrading a package for one project can
    silently break another

Introduction to Python Environments


   • A Python environment is a workspace where Python and its
    packages are installed and managed for a project

   •  Separate environments help avoid conflicts between package
    versions and project dependencies

   • Key topics covered: virtual environments, venv, pip and
    requirements.txt

   • Used throughout real-world development to keep projects
    reproducible and portable

What is a Virtual Environment?


  • An isolated directory containing a Python interpreter and a separate
    package installation area

  •  Python provides the built-in venv module for creating virtual
    environments

  • No extra installation needed — venv ships with Python 3.3 and later

  • Each environment behaves like its own self-contained Python installation

Creating a Virtual Environment


  •  Navigate to the project directory first

  •  Create an environment using venv:

    python -m venv myenv

  •  This creates a folder named myenv containing the interpreter and
   package directories

  • Environment names such as myenv, venv or .venv are common
   conventions

    source myenv/bin/activate

  • Runs pip using the specifically selected Python interpreter

  • Reduces confusion when multiple Python installations or

    different one

Source slide page 15 (extracted text):
Python For Computational Problem Solving
Virtual Environment vs System Python


  • System Python: packages are shared across many projects, so
    conflicts are more likely

  •  Virtual environment: packages are isolated per project,
   minimizing conflicts

  • Changes to system Python can affect the whole machine; venv
   changes stay contained

  •  Best practice: always develop inside a project-specific virtual
   environment
